# Donald Knuth: Key Information
Donald Knuth is an influential computer scientist and writer, best known for *The Art of Computer Programming* (TAOCP), a seminal multi-volume work regarded as foundational in computer science. Knuth began work on TAOCP in the early 1960s, intending it as a single book, but expanded the project to encompass multiple volumes due to the depth of the subject. The first volume was published in 1968, and subsequent volumes have been released over the decades, with ongoing work on future installments. His writing style emphasizes storytelling as an effective means of communication, and he has contributed to recreational mathematics and authored *Surreal Numbers* and other texts. Knuth proposed the term "algorithmics" for computer science and contributed forewords and puzzles to various publications.
Knuth created the digital typesetting systems TeX and Metafont after becoming dissatisfied with the phototypesetting quality for TAOCP. He pioneered "literate programming," advocating that programs should primarily explain to humans what the computer is meant to do, and developed the WEB and CWEB systems to support this approach. Knuth is also known for his humor, such as giving hexadecimal-based rewards for errors found in his books. His personal interests include music composition, organ performance, and calligraphy, as evidenced by his religious text publications. He served as professor at Stanford University and was a visiting professor at Oxford. Knuth has received numerous prestigious awards, including the ACM Turing Award, National Medal of Science, John von Neumann Medal, Kyoto Prize, and many others, recognizing his fundamental contributions to mathematics, computer science, and digital publishing.
